summary: This informational memo presents a problem statement for access rate measurement test protocols used with IP Performance Metrics (IPPM). It discusses key aspects such as controlling the packet characteristics on the tested path and states requirements for such a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This document says what a protocol has to be able to do before it can measure how fast someone's Internet link really is. It sets out the roles of the sending and receiving devices, the kinds of test traffic a protocol can send, and which of them are required.

questions: how to measure access rate ippm
how to measure internet access rate
subtitle: What a protocol must be able to do to measure how fast an Internet access link really is.

tldr.problem: People comparing one Internet access offer with another need a common way to measure the rate a link really delivers, and there was no agreed statement of what such a measurement protocol has to be able to do.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes the access rate problem, the roles of sender, receiver and reporter, and four ways of generating test traffic, then states which of them a test protocol must support and which it may offer.
tldr.outcome: It names one form of traffic generation as required and treats the rest as optional, and it points out that the standardised test protocols of the day cannot generate different packet sizes in each direction.

facts.label: Stream generation categories
facts.value: 4, of which only ensembles are required

facts.label: Required asymmetry
facts.value: Asymmetric packet rates in a two-way architecture

today: RFC 7497 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it stands as a statement of the access rate measurement problem rather than a standard. It leaves the design of any actual measurement protocol to later work.

sections.title: Why the Access Rate Is Worth Measuring
sections.content:
There are many possible rate measurement scenarios. This memo describes one of them and presents a rate measurement problem statement for test protocols that measure IP Performance Metrics (IPPM), the framework that sets out how a network's performance can be measured.

The starting point is a subscriber choosing between ways of getting access to the Internet. The subscriber wants to compare the performance of the alternatives, and standardised measurements are what make that comparison possible. That creates a need to coordinate measurements that support such comparisons, and to test the control protocols that would fulfil the need. The document sketches the typical measurement points of an access network: a user device or host reaches an access node over fibre, copper or radio, and from there the infrastructure leads to a gateway.

The access rate scenario has drawn attention from Internet-access subscribers and, the document says, from seemingly all the players in the Internet industry, including regulators. It is being approached with many different measurement methods. The eventual protocol solutions, and the systems that use them, may not involve users directly, because a test can run from the infrastructure to a service-specific device such as a residential gateway. Nothing in the problem, however, stops users from writing a test protocol driven by command line interfaces at both ends. The range of possible outcomes is therefore wide: test protocols, active measurement methods, and whole systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The document starts from something ordinary: people comparing Internet access offers want to know which one is really faster. To compare fairly, the measurements have to be made the same way and coordinated between the two ends. The memo is the statement of what that measurement has to achieve.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The scope is to define the measurement problem statement for test protocols conducting access rate measurement on production networks. Two relevant test protocols are named, the one-way active measurement protocol in RFC 4656 and the two-way active measurement protocol in RFC 5357, but the problem is stated generally enough that any existing test protocol, such as the one in RFC 6812, can address it. The memo discusses possible measurement methods but does not specify the exact methods that would normally be part of the solution.

The scenarios of interest share several characteristics. The access portion of the network is the focus. The user typically subscribes to a service with bidirectional access, partly described by rates in bits per second; those rates may be expressed as raw capacity or as restricted capacity, as described in RFC 6703. Possible measurement points, following the reference path defined in RFC 7398, are a subscriber's host, the access service demarcation point, the intra IP access point where a globally routable address is present, or the gateway between the measured access network and other networks. Rates on links near the edge of a provider's network are often several orders of magnitude lower than link rates in the aggregation and core. Asymmetrical access rates on ingress and egress are prevalent. Services of extremely large scale tend to use low-complexity devices at the user end, and those devices limit clock and control timing accuracy. The problem statement assumes the most likely bottleneck device or link sits next to the remote, user-end measurement device or within one or two router or switch hops of it.

There is also an aggregated leased-network case, where one operator leases packet switching and transport facilities from another and the available link capacity cannot be read directly from device interface utilisation. Mobile backhaul, Ethernet service access networks and layer 2 or layer 3 extensions are all in scope. The results could be used to select alternate routing, to check whether capacity meets a previous agreement, or to adapt the rate of traffic sources when a bottleneck is found. In this case the tester is assumed to control both the sender and the receiver location.

Two things are explicitly non-goals: solving the measurement protocol specification problem, and standardising methods of measurement. Even so, the problem statement mandates support for one category of rate measurement methods in the test protocol, together with adequate control features for the methods in the control protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The measurement focuses on the access link itself, where speeds are lowest and often different in each direction. Tests may run from a subscriber's own machine, from the point where the provider's network begins, or from a gateway. The memo also covers a second case: one provider leasing capacity from another, where the real capacity cannot simply be read off a device.

sections.title: Active Rate Measurement and Its Three Roles
sections.content:
The memo describes active measurement, which uses synthetic traffic streams dedicated to testing rather than measuring real user traffic. Coordination between the source and destination devices through control messages is taken as given, following the IPPM documents that define it.

Most active testing intrudes on user performance to some degree, especially when it happens while service is in use. One key tenet of IPPM methods is to minimise the effect of test traffic on user traffic. The most relevant problems are the tendency of measurement traffic to skew the results, followed by the possibility of causing congestion on the access link. Anyone using a protocol for in-service testing must respect those traffic constraints. Categories of measurement method that use less active test traffic than others with similar accuracy are therefore preferred, and the memo encourages traffic reduction through asymmetric control capabilities.

Out-of-service tests, where the test path shares no links with in-service user traffic, have none of the congestion or skew concerns, although both kinds of test have to complete within a reasonable time from the tester's point of view and keep timestamp accuracy consistent with the precision the measurement needs. Where part of an out-of-service test path is shared with in-service traffic, the in-service constraints apply again.

The architecture may be one-way, as in RFC 4656, or two-way, as in RFC 5357. The scale and complexity of end-user or aggregated access measurement clearly favour the two-way form, with a low-complexity device at the user end and results collected round trip. Because the rates of many access services are asymmetric, the measurement system must be able to evaluate performance in each direction of transmission; in a two-way architecture both end devices must be able to launch test streams and collect measurement results in both directions.

Three roles are named. The SENDER generates streams of test packets with the chosen characteristics and may sit at the user end of the access path or elsewhere in the production network, such as at one end of an aggregated leased-network segment. The RECEIVER collects the test packet streams and makes the measurements needed at its end of the access or leased segment. The REPORTER uses information from the test packets and from local processes to measure delivered packet rates and prepare the results in the required format; the REPORTER role may be combined with another role, most likely the SENDER.
sections.plainLanguage: Testing while a service is in use can distort the very numbers it tries to measure and can slow the link down, so the rules for test traffic are strict. The memo then splits the job into three parts: sending test packets, receiving them, and turning what arrived into a report.

sections.title: Four Ways of Generating Test Traffic
sections.content:
A protocol that addresses the rate measurement problem must serve the test stream generation and measurement functions, the SENDER and the RECEIVER. The phase that analyses the results to produce a report sits outside the scope of the memo and is the REPORTER's job.

The memo groups the many possible forms of test stream into four categories. First, packet pairs with fixed spacing inside a pair and fixed or random intervals between pairs. Second, multiple streams of packet pairs with a range of spacing inside and between pairs. Third, packet ensembles, using a fixed number of packets per ensemble and one or more fixed spacings inside it; zero spacing counts here, so back-to-back burst ensembles and constant rate ensembles both fall into this category. Fourth, packet chirps, sets of packets with specified characteristics in which the spacing between adjacent packets typically decreases, with each pair representing a rate for testing purposes.

The test protocol must support test packet ensemble generation, category three, because it appears to minimise the demands on measurement accuracy. The other categories are optional. Across all supported categories, the protocol must be able to specify, control and generate variable payload lengths among packet streams; variable length in packets among streams or ensembles; variable IP header markings; a choice of UDP transport with variable port numbers, or TCP transport with variable port numbers for two-way architectures only, or both; and a variable number of packet pairs, ensembles or streams in a test session. Revising those variables during an established test session is optional, as is generating streams with VLAN tags and other markings.

Measurement systems that use TCP need a sender able to establish and prime the connection so that the desired stream characteristics are permitted. Such an open-loop TCP sender must generate TCP packets with well-formed headers, with all fields valid including the acknowledgement aspects; produce packet streams at controlled rates and variable inter-packet spacings, including ensembles sent back to back at the server rate; and continue the configured sending characteristics despite all control indications except receive-window exhaustion. The matching TCP receiver performs normally, but needs the ability to configure its receive window large enough for the sender to transmit at will, up to a configured target.

Measurements for each UDP test packet moved between SENDER and RECEIVER must comply with the singleton measurement methods in the IPPM documents RFC 2679 and RFC 2680. The timestamp information, or the loss and arrival status, for each packet must be available for communication to the REPORTER function.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists four shapes a test stream can take, from pairs of packets sent a fixed time apart to chirps in which the gap shrinks step by step. Only one is required: ensembles, where a fixed number of packets is sent together. A protocol must also be able to vary payload length, packet count, IP header markings, transport protocol and port numbers.

sections.title: What the Test Protocol Must Do
sections.content:
Section 5 collects the requirements. The test protocol must communicate all test variables to the SENDER and the RECEIVER; it must support results collection in a one-way architecture; it must support remote device control for both one-way and two-way architectures; and it must support asymmetric packet rates in a two-way measurement architecture, or coordinated one-way test capabilities with the same effect, with asymmetric rates achieved through directional control of packet rate or packet size.

The ability to control and generate asymmetric rates in a two-way architecture is required. Two-way architectures are recommended to include control and generation capability for both asymmetric and symmetric packet sizes, because packet size often matters in this problem, and test systems should be able to detect directional size dependency through comparative measurements.

Asymmetric packet size control is indicated when the result of a measurement may depend on the size of the packets used in each direction. The memo lists the situations that call for it: a link in the path with asymmetrical capacity in opposite directions; a link that aggregates packets into link-level frames and may have a capacity that depends on packet size, rate or timing; a link where transmission in one direction influences performance in the opposite direction; a device whose transmission capacity depends on packet header processing capacity; a target application stream of nominally MTU size packets in one direction against an acknowledgement stream in the other; and a case where the distribution of packet losses is critical to the rate assessment. Implementations may support control and generation for only symmetric packet sizes when none of those conditions hold.

The test protocol should enable measurement of the capacity metric of RFC 5136, either out-of-service, in-service, or both. Other metrics from that document are optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol has to pass every test setting to both ends, let an operator control the remote device, and be able to send at different rates in each direction. Different packet sizes in each direction matter whenever the link itself treats small and large packets differently, and the memo lists the cases where that can happen.

sections.title: Security and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations that apply to any active measurement of live networks apply here as well, and the memo points to the two-way and one-way active measurement protocols for them. Privacy considerations for measurement systems, particularly where Internet users take part in the tests, are described in the LMAP framework. There is also a risk that a proprietary service level agreement with the access network segment provider leaks during a rate measurement, so test protocols should not convey that information in a way that unauthorised parties could discover.

Operationally, all forms of testing originate network traffic, either through the control and results collection messages, through dedicated measurement packet streams, or through a combination of the two. Testing traffic falls mainly into one of two categories, subscriber traffic or network management traffic. There is an ongoing need to engineer networks so that the various forms of traffic are adequately served, and publishing the memo does not change that need. Service subscribers and authorised users should obtain their network operator's or service provider's permission before conducting tests. A service provider or third party should obtain the subscriber's permission, since testing might temporarily reduce service quality. The protocol should communicate the permission status once the overall system has obtained it, either explicitly or by other means.

Capacity testing with active traffic often affects the packet transfer performance of streams that share parts of the test path. The degradation can be minimised by scheduling such tests infrequently and restricting the amount of measurement traffic needed to assess capacity metrics. Occasional short-duration estimates with minimal traffic are therefore preferred to measurements based on frequent file transfers of many megabytes with similar accuracy. The memo notes that the scheduled frequency of testing matters as much as the methods used, and that schedules are not typically submitted for standardisation.

The memo recommends the new feature of asymmetric packet size generation in two-way testing, because it reduces the load and the packet processing demands of each test and so reduces the likelihood of degradation in one direction of the tested path. It observes that the standardised test protocols of the day, the two-way protocol in RFC 5357 and the protocol in RFC 6812, do not have that capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Running a test puts real traffic on the network, so the memo says to get permission from the subscriber and from the operator first, and to keep the test short and small rather than moving large files repeatedly. It ends by pointing out that the standardised protocols of the time cannot send different packet sizes in each direction.

viz.caption: The four categories of test stream generation in Section 4

items.title: Packet pairs
items.text: Fixed spacing inside a pair, fixed or random intervals between pairs.

items.title: Multiple streams of pairs
items.text: A range of spacing inside pairs and a range of intervals between them.

items.title: Packet ensembles
items.text: Fixed ensemble size with fixed spacings inside, including zero spacing. The only required category.

items.title: Packet chirps
items.text: Spacing between adjacent packets typically decreases; each pair represents a rate to test.

viz.caption: The two testing situations described in Section 2

left.title: In-service testing
left.desc: Takes place with user traffic present, so test traffic can skew the result and can cause congestion on the access link.

right.title: Out-of-service testing
right.desc: Takes place during pre-service assessment or planned maintenance, with no user traffic on the test path.
